processes.description: In the autumn the logistics budget coordinator opens the next year's budget: she announces when the first draft is due, sends managers a budget questionnaire to fill in and return by a deadline, and asks them to list their staff by position. Managers reply with their headcount, sometimes a one-person region, and later send revised forecasts after working through staffing with HR. Through the year, final monthly budget numbers and regional budget-versus-actual comparison reports go out as attachments to the cost center managers.
steps: The coordinator announces the next year's budget cycle and the due date for the first draft.
Managers receive a budget questionnaire to complete and return by the stated deadline.
Managers list their staff by position and offer salary detail if it is needed.
Managers revise their budget after reviewing staffing with HR and send a revised forecast.
Final monthly budget numbers are circulated once the month is closed.
Budget-versus-actual comparison reports are sent to the regional cost center managers.

stalls.summary: A manager's budget went round again: revisions followed a session with the HR department, and a revised forecast was sent the next day, so the submission was reworked after the first version.
Regional budget-versus-actual comparison reports arrived bundled for several past months at once, well after those months had closed, which suggests the monthly reporting falls behind.

automation.approach: A standard budget workbook sent at the start of the cycle, prefilled with each manager's current positions from HR records, so managers confirm and adjust staffing instead of listing staff and answering the questionnaire from scratch; budget-versus-actual reports generated from the ledger at month close and sent to each cost center manager on a fixed schedule.
automation.rationale: The repeated hands-on work is filling in a questionnaire, listing positions and reworking forecasts after checking staffing with HR; a prefilled form removes the re-keying and much of the rework. The monthly reports are a mechanical extract that a scheduled report can produce, which would also stop them arriving in bundles.

work_estimate.rationale: Minutes go to completing the budget questionnaire, listing staff positions, reworking the forecast after checking staffing with HR, and assembling monthly budget or budget-versus-actual reports. A one-person region needs about 15 minutes; a full revised forecast with HR input can take up to 180 minutes; 60 minutes is a typical round. Prefilled headcount and generated reports could take over the data entry and report assembly, while managers still judge staffing and spend.

processes.description: The pipeline commercial team plans its strategy around expansions, interconnects and storage projects. A round starts with a customer or project question, such as an interconnect, a storage project or a fuel charge, or with a call for a strategy meeting. Facility Planning prepares cost estimates and spreadsheets for build, expansion and interconnect cases, revises them when Marketing asks for costs split out, and economics are run on them. Assistants and managers schedule and reschedule strategy meetings where scenarios, risks and customer proposals are discussed.
steps: A manager or assistant calls a strategy meeting and confirms the date, time and room.
Marketing raises a customer or project request, such as an interconnect or storage project, and names a contact.
Facility Planning prepares cost estimates and spreadsheets for build, expansion or interconnect cases.
Estimates are revised on Marketing's request, for example splitting out interest, overheads and AFUDC.
Economics are run on the costs and negotiating parameters such as fuel charges are settled.
The team meets on scenarios, benefits, risks and strategy, and proposals go out to customers.

stalls.summary: Cost estimates wait on facility information from field staff: work on an interconnect estimate was held up pending data from the Roswell office.
Supporting material is slow to obtain: getting a map showing the power plant proved more difficult than expected.
Meetings are moved and re-polled: a strategy meeting was moved, attendees were asked which dates suit them and to reply all, people answered with alternative days, and room changes were sent out.

Cost spreadsheets go round again: revised versions follow the previous day's spreadsheet, and estimates are reworked when Marketing asks for interest, overheads and AFUDC split out for all line items.
A commercial lead was left without negotiating parameters for the fuel charge on a project and had to ask for them.
Who handles an interconnect is settled ad hoc: a colleague is asked whether they have time to take it on and to tell the other party they are the marketing contact.

automation.approach: A standard cost-estimate workbook for interconnect, lateral and expansion cases, with interest, overheads and AFUDC split out by default and a version label on each issue, plus a shared project tracker listing each project's owner, marketing contact and outstanding field data, and a standing strategy meeting slot with an agenda.
automation.rationale: The rework in the mail centres on cost spreadsheets being revised and resent and on facility data awaited from the field; a fixed workbook layout and a tracker of open items address both. Engineering judgement, economics and negotiating positions stay with people.

work_estimate.rationale: Minutes go mainly to Facility Planning's cost estimates and spreadsheets for expansion, pipeline build and bi-directional interconnect cases, their revisions, and the economics run on them, plus preparing for strategy meetings. A round that only sets up a meeting needs about 15 minutes of preparation; a full cost estimate with revisions can run to 240 minutes; 60 minutes is a typical round across the mix. A standard workbook could take over layout, cost splitting and version handling, not the engineering or negotiating judgement.

processes.description: The gas logistics desks prepare to work from a backup location. Managers are asked how many desks they need on the backup floor, backup seats are assigned and the list of team members given spots is circulated, and a memo asks schedulers to fill in survey data from their desk spreadsheets on how nominations would be made remotely, including which pipelines require or can use dial-up access to their electronic bulletin boards.
steps: A manager asks each desk lead how many desks they need at the backup location.
Backup seats are allocated and the list of team members given spots is circulated.
A memo goes to desk managers asking their schedulers to fill in survey data from their desk spreadsheets.
Responses are compiled into a list of pipelines that require or can use dial-up EBB access.

automation.approach: A continuity roster workbook per desk, kept current, holding backup seat assignments, desk counts and, for each pipeline, how nominations are submitted remotely, including dial-up EBB access, so each planning round or seat test starts from the existing roster and only changes are collected.
automation.rationale: Each round re-collects the same facts, seat counts, names and pipeline access methods, by memo and desk spreadsheet; a maintained roster turns that into a review of changes. Seat testing and the decisions on who gets a backup spot remain with the managers.

work_estimate.rationale: Minutes go to counting desk needs, allocating backup seats and compiling the list of people given spots, and to schedulers filling in each pipeline's remote nomination method from desk spreadsheets and compiling the dial-up list. A seat count alone takes about 15 minutes; a desk-wide survey compiled across pipelines can take 120 minutes; 45 minutes is a typical round. A maintained roster could take over the re-collection and compiling, while seat decisions stay with managers.
